title: DAWN_AND_YEAR_test
about: A test film for the editor: the two alignment acts of script v3.1 built only from clips that exist today (production_examples.zip). Same shot-file schema as films/stonehenge/stonehenge.shots.json, plus: key_instant (HH:MM:SS on the shot's own light span, from the record: first gleam 03:48:46, half disc 03:51:27, whole 03:54:07; midwinter sits 16:03:04, half-set 16:05:42, gone 16:08:26), style (a directors.json row), and film.target_seconds. Handles: rendered shots carry 24 frames (1 s) each side (make_v3.js HAND=24); A_axis_5s has none; the contrast inserts are held clips.

shots.proves: at the solstice sunrise every shadow lies down the axis
shots.voice: Seen from above, at sunrise on the longest day, every stone throws its shadow the same way — south-west, straight down the monument's axis.

shots.proves: only the summer solstice lies on the axis (same Sun height 3°: summer, autumn, winter, spring)
shots.voice: On any other morning, the shadows point elsewhere.

shots.proves: the first light of the solstice inside the Great Trilithon's slot
shots.voice: Stand on that line and look back north-east. The first light of the solstice appears inside the slot of the Great Trilithon.

shots.proves: the equinox Sun sets at a gap's edge, not inside one (D56)
shots.voice: Not every day is marked. At the equinox the Sun sets due west — at the edge of a gap, not inside one.

shots.proves: in the midwinter afternoon the shadows run up the axis to the Heel Stone
shots.voice: Six months on, the shadows turn round. In the low winter afternoon they run north-east, up the same axis.

shots.proves: only the winter solstice evening lies on the axis
the same slot from the other side takes the midwinter sunset
shots.voice: The axis works both ways. From the other side, the midwinter Sun goes down through the same slot.

shots.proves: Station Stones' long side 319.8° vs northernmost moonset 319.2° at the major standstill of -2498
shots.voice: Four smaller stones mark a rectangle. Its long side points north-west — to where the Moon sets at its northernmost, once every 18.6 years.
